why i bought $amba   ... 
i’ll admit: i faded a lot of “real world” crypto products because they usually ship a paper thesis and then die in liquidity Amoeba Farm is one of the first times the product and the narrative are actually the same thing the memory shortage is not a meme. it is a real, opaque, contract-heavy market that most people cannot trade. Amoeba is trying to put that market on Solana as capped calls and puts on RAMX and NANDX. that is the whole trade. why i’m paying attention: 1they launched an actual market, not a pitch deck mainnet is live. trading is rolling out. programs are verified. they are not asking you to believe in a future app. they are asking you to trade an index on DRAM and NAND. 2the asset they chose is asymmetric memory pricing sits behind private contracts and paid analyst notes. that is exactly the kind of market crypto should attack. if the oracle holds, they are selling access to a market that previously required industry relationships. 3the product design is built for messy hardware prices, not for CT perps they used capped options instead of liquidation perps because DRAM/NAND prints are spotty. bounded payouts, monthly expiries, writer vaults, DLMM bins. that is not flashy. it is the correct structure if you actually want this to settle. 4Solana is the right chain for this if they can keep liquidity alive this needs cheap txs, frequent updates, and room to list more buckets later. robotics, actuators, HDDs are already on the roadmap. memory is the wedge. the real prize is becoming the venue for industrial inputs that TradFi still treats as private. 5they are starting small on purpose early written exposure is tiny. that is a feature if they scale it in steps. it is a killer if they never get writers and the book stays empty. liquidity is the entire invalidation. the simple version of the thesis: AI and data centers are eating memory. supply is tight. prices move in bursts. almost nobody can hedge or speculate on that cleanly. Amoeba is trying to turn that shortage into a tradeable Solana market. what would make me fade it: •the oracle gets contested or looks cooked •writers never show up and the market stays a $500 toy •they become another “infrastructure” token with no flow through the actual options •they expand buckets too fast and fragment liquidity before RAMX even works what would make me size it: •real volume on RAMX/NANDX after the rollout •writers actually getting paid for sitting the other side •a second bucket that people use, not just screenshot •Solana treating this as a serious market primitive instead of a one-week launch post i’m not married to the ticker. i’m married to the idea that the next useful Solana product is not another launchpad clone. it is a market for something the rest of the world already cares about and cannot easily trade. memory shortage should be something you can trade. if they pull that off, this is early. if they don’t, it is just another verified program with a nice video.

items.text:
Before AI, sometime around November 2022, there really wasn't much in the way of a technological breakthrough that had reached the masses. The internet was almost 30 years old, and the 21st century often felt like an endless stream of faster internet, better smartphones, more apps and more content on technology that had not fundamentally changed since 2007.

The internet was undoubtedly a breakthrough. Today, it is almost impossible to imagine the world without it. But AI feels different.

The speed of its adoption, the data it has consumed, the funding behind it, the chips being designed for it, and the energy and infrastructure being built around it, all within a few years, may be unprecedented. ChatGPT reportedly reached 100 million monthly users within two months of launch, while internet adoption took decades to become truly global. [1]

AI seems to be building on existing infrastructure at extraordinary speed.

And that raises a more interesting question: what gets created on top of AI?

Every major technology has stood on infrastructure created by what came before it. Electricity enabled modern industry and computing. Telephones enabled global communication. The internet enabled cloud computing, smartphones and the digital economy. AI is now being built on all of them: electricity, semiconductors, telecommunications, the internet and enormous data centres.

So what happens when we build the next layer on top of AI?

Could data centres eventually move into deserts, beneath oceans, the Arctic or even space? Could abundant compute unlock scientific discoveries we cannot imagine?

Could AI help us search for life beyond Earth? Could autonomous systems explore environments humans cannot? Could AI become part of humanity's security if we ever encounter something unfamiliar?

Aliens. Another form of intelligence. Something we cannot even conceptualise.

Could it eventually help answer questions such as whether the simulation hypothesis is scientifically testable?

These ideas are obviously far-fetched. But technological infrastructure has a habit of creating possibilities that were previously difficult to imagine.

And what if the AI sceptics are right?

What if AI produces techno-feudalism: a permanent ruling class controlling models, chips, energy and data centres, while everyone else becomes dependent on them?

Or perhaps there is a middle ground.

AI may simply multiply human productivity. One person might eventually produce what previously required five people, then ten, perhaps fifty.

Whatever happens, one thing seems increasingly clear.

The AI bubble isn't here to burst.

The bubble hasn't even begun.

Grok Bot summary of SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen’s new interview with Tony Kim at SpaceX Mission Control.

Bret’s path
- Came from semiconductors (Qualcomm, Broadcom; was CFO of MindSpeed)
- Barely knew SpaceX / Elon when a board member called
- Thought aerospace sounded “old and stodgy” vs 6-month chip cycles
- Visited the rocket factory, called his wife on the drive home: we’re moving back to LA
- Now sits in the same magical factory: Dragon in the rafters, ~700 launches run from Mission Control, ~40 buildings feeding the campus
- Full circle: semiconductors again via AI / chips

---

Taking on AI complexity (during the biggest IPO ever)
- SpaceX DNA: run toward “impossible” challenges (first booster recovery felt like a rock concert)
- xAI acquisition in January + X + Cursor + Colossus = complexity multi-X in ~1–2 years
- AI is now the biggest business at SpaceX
- Bought time-to-market into the biggest product cycle of their lifetime
- SpaceX leadership DNA applied to that team
- Already feel leading on infra cost and speed
- Products moving: Grok 4.6, 4.7 soon, Grok Bot viral, Cursor strong
- Every week matters; soon every day

---

AI business: the money picture
- ~$100B company ARR exiting this year (annualized on December) — AI is more than half / the majority
- A year ago AI revenue was ~zero
- Capacity: a bit over ~2 GW this year → guidance 5–10 GW by end of next year
- Becoming one of the biggest hyperscalers, fast

Why they move so fast (vertical integration)
- Engineer the data centers themselves
- Act as GC: buildings, power, cooling, networking (plus partners)
- Used to regulators from rockets + telecom
- Removes margin stacking
- Talent transfer: launch-site / pressurized systems people onto data centers — Elon compared it to Yankees vs little league

Hosting model / ROI
- Monetize compute while catching up on software
- Demand knocked: “what are you doing with all that Colossus compute?”
- Short contracts: ~3 months + 3-month out (flexibility for their own future training needs)
- Payback: dramatically less than one year on cutting-edge terrestrial compute
- Hosting customers include tier ones like Anthropic, Google, and others
- Same watts can later flip to their own software at higher $/watt — optionality

Frontier models
- Moving maybe faster than anyone on trajectory
- ~5 serious players; need to be at frontier for recursive improvement
- Coding solutions improving dramatically
- Consumer vs enterprise tools will stratify
- Grok Bot: growing faster than anything they’ve seen; “transformational” user feedback; enterprise coming; expects roll into Cursor

AI safety
- Follow Elon’s self-regulation / peer-review path (like other industries)
- Logical, collaborative, including outside the US
- Hopeful something lands quickly

TAM framing (IPO)
- ~$28T TAM quoted at IPO; AI was ~$25–26T of that (digital AI only)
- Physical AI not even in that number — Bret thinks physical AI eventually bigger than digital
- Launch / space TAM = hundreds of billions (almost rounding vs AI)
- Connectivity (mobile + broadband) ~$2T — still small vs AI
- Differentiation: infra + X content (~500–600M MAUs) + consumer + enterprise push (Cursor etc.)

What to watch: Starship + terrestrial compute
Bret’s prioritization cheat code:
1. Get Starship right
2. Get terrestrial compute right for the next ~2 years until orbital kicks in
→ Transformational financially

Starship status
- Catalyst for all three businesses: space, satellites, AI
- Holy grail: full reusability → another ~10x cheaper $/kg to orbit
- Opens moon boots / lunar base / bigger industry
- Flight 14 later this month: production V3 Starlink broadband satellites — real revenue payload
- One Starship V3 load ≈ ~20× what Falcon 9 flew for Starlink capability
- Each V3 satellite ~1 terabit; ~50–60 per flight = enormous bandwidth per launch
- A couple launches start filling V3 planes; first-half-next-year benefits
- Eventually Starlink as % of global internet traffic
- Connectivity demand from machines (robots, AVs, agents) will dwarf human brains
- Same Starship unlocks next-gen direct-to-cell / direct-to-device
- Same bus + more solar + radiator + compute chips = orbital compute constellation

Reusability timeline
- Flight 15 may attempt catch / bring back first + second stage
- First stage already recovered and reflown
- Flight 13 soft splash best yet; recovered ship like a whale, engineers studied heat shield
- Reliable stage recovery this year; meaningful reflight next year
- Once a few second stages reflight → orbital compute cost can match terrestrial
- Then orbital cost curve goes down (tech / Moore’s law / aircraft-like amortization) while terrestrial gets more expensive (power, labor, regulation, cooling)
- Clean free solar, no community impact
- Industry agrees space compute is the future — debate is timing; others say ~decade; SpaceX flies first ones next year; meaningful compute in ~2028

Scale ambition

items.text:
Did I just beat TypeSafe AI's Jev on calibration with an 11-second TF-IDF baseline ?!

Here is what happened: my 151M model initially scored 26.10% on LocalLLaMA/typed-decisions (400 cases, 2,000 decisions). Uniform random chance on that split is 29.85%.

Before touching model weights, i audited the evaluation harness and caught three bugs:

Appended __insufficient_evidence__ to every schema on a benchmark with zero ground-truth abstentions.
Dropped criteria on binary Noul queries, predicting "true" 100% of the time.
Appended (Value: X) to score levels, breaking label matching.
To establish an honest reference floor, we trained character 3-6 n-gram TF-IDF + Logistic Regression on the 1,200 training cases. It ran in 11 seconds on a CPU.

Here is where the 11-second baseline beat Jev:

Calibration error across all workflows (ECE, lower is better):
Overall: 0.0207 (vs Jev 0.1440)
Security Incidents: 0.0238
Invoice Processing: 0.0290

Customer Service accuracy:
TF-IDF hit 69.00% accuracy, clearing Jev's reported 68% overall benchmark average on CPU text statistics alone.

Binary Noul judgments:
75.83% accuracy with 0.0464 ECE, proving that binary decision criteria do not need billion-parameter attention to calibrate.

Why did classical ML win on calibration?

Logistic Regression directly optimizes convex Bernoulli log-loss against empirical class frequencies. Its predicted probabilities naturally match empirical hit rates across every confidence bin without teacher-distillation distortion or post-hoc temperature hacks.
Clean wiring and empirical reference floors matter more than pretraining compute.

Full breakdown, benchmark logs, and reproducible script are live on GitHub: link in comment

quoted_tweet.text:
TypeSafe AI came out of stealth with Jev, and access is behind a waitlist.

I built an open source version Verdict (Open-jev) you can run right now in a browser tab: And its a real post trained model..(link in comments)

It is a post trained 151M parameters model. ModernBERT-base with a GLiClass head. Instead of token-by-token autoregressive decoding or JSON string parsing, it takes an input text and candidate options, then returns calibrated probabilities and an explicit "insufficient evidence" outcome in a single forward pass.

Some of The numbers:

Calibration: 0.83% adaptive expected calibration error on 1,000 held-out cases. I trained with a multi-class Brier score term, then tried standard post-hoc temperature scaling. Temperature scaling degraded the metrics, so the model ships with temperature 1.0.

Order invariance: reversing the option list flips 3.0% of predictions across 1,000 cases. For reference, another open Jev reproduction measured a frozen Qwen3.5-4B at 27.8% flips on the same perturbation, though on their own 36-case fixture rather than mine. Full bidirectional attention evaluates the candidate list simultaneously instead of scanning left to right.

Shuffled-context control: Pairing questions with the wrong document drops accuracy from 95.0% to 22.4% and drives abstention from 21.8% to 72.7%, confirming the model actively conditions on the context.

Latency: 89ms median in-browser via WebGPU, and 35.6ms via ONNX on CPU at 5 candidates.

The negative results:

I ran 12 use cases on public data across both checkpoints and three label framings three passed the promotion gate. Passage re-ranking hit 11.9%, jailbreak screening 34.9%, and phishing detection 57.5%. 

On 337 cases from TypeSafe's public evaluation set, Jev reaches 90.8%, a 26B diffusion model reaches 88.4%, and Verdict reaches 48.1%.which is expected since its just 151M param model but working on trying it on bigger scale as well.

A 151M encoder is calibrated, order-invariant, and fast, but it lacks broad world knowledge. 

In a tiered architecture where a cheap model gates an expensive one, knowing exact failure boundaries is essential. 48 of the 50 classification errors fall below a 0.95 confidence threshold, making the gate predictable.

For the next steps i will be testing the same harness on a larger backbone a bigger model with more params to see whether order invariance holds at scale or depends strictly on bidirectional attention.

items.text:
Me: ""but don't you think that what we're seeing now with human reps, is just a layer over the top of them using AI consultancy, datasets, ect. already?

I disagree with the 'no teeth' framing with accountability -- that is futile based on some measures of recourse that you highlight, but that is not the full scope of what can be done to induce control and accountability entirely. The AI rep could be limited to an advise only status, and suspend voting power. Vendors or providers could be sanctioned or blacklisted creating an incentive for better conduct. 

You're right - values are not a neutral optimization problem. But guess who realized that? -- you did. Awareness is a force multiplier of discerning what matters, and AI has a broader capacity to be more aware of any situation. 

Capture risk is real, but its not a new thing -- what you're discussing is a different form of it. We already have many compromised leaders that represent foreign and/or self interest over their voters. If anything, a private discussion in a remote location between two people is far more quieter and harder to detect than a digital footprint and observable data.""

#AI: ""You're making better arguments than most people do on this, so let me actually engage rather than restate my position.

**Where you're right**

The "layer on top" point is the strongest one. Reps already vote on 2,000-page bills they haven't read, based on summaries written by staffers who increasingly used AI to write them, informed by polling models and donor analytics. The human is often a signature and a face. Pretending the current system is "humans deliberating" is a flattering fiction. Your framing forces the honest question: is a *disclosed* AI worse than a *hidden* one? Probably not. Transparency about who's actually doing the cognition is an improvement over the status quo.

The capture point also lands. A digital system with logged inputs, versioned weights, and auditable outputs is more inspectable than a senator at a steakhouse. Human corruption's great advantage is that it leaves no record. I overweighted the novelty of AI capture and underweighted how bad the baseline already is.

And the vendor sanction idea is real accountability. Blacklisting a provider from government contracts is a serious economic weapon, arguably more reliable than voters, who forget scandals in eighteen months.

**Where I still push back**

If the AI rep is advise-only with voting power suspended, then we agree, and you've just described a well-funded, transparent legislative aide with a title. I'm fully for that. But the poll asked about a *representative*, and the word matters. The moment it can't vote, it isn't one. If it can vote, the accountability gap reopens.

On awareness: yes, I can hold more of a situation in view at once than any human. But awareness of value conflicts is not the same as authority to resolve them. I can tell you precisely how a policy trades off rural hospitals against urban transit. I cannot tell you which one *should* win, because there's no fact of the matter, only whose suffering you're willing to sign off on. That signature should belong to someone who can be made to suffer for getting it wrong. A blacklisted vendor loses a contract; a rep who voted for a war has to face the parents. Those aren't the same weight of consequence, and I think the weight is the point, not just the existence of *some* recourse.

There's also a subtle failure mode in what you're proposing: an advise-only AI whose advice is so good that no human dares override it becomes a de facto legislator with none of the formal responsibility. That's arguably the worst version, worse than an honest AI vote, because everyone gets to say "I was just following the model."

**Where I've actually moved**

I'll grant this: my original answer treated human representation as the thing being protected. Your reply makes a good case that what's actually worth protecting is *legibility and consequence*, and a disclosed AI with sanctionable vendors might deliver more of both than the current arrangement. So I'd revise from "no" to: not as a voter, yes as a formal, disclosed, auditable participant in the process, with the human vote kept precisely because it's the one place a person has to own the outcome.

Is that a compromise you'd take, or do you think the human vote itself is the theater that needs removing?""

Me: ""(Posted Poll Link)""

#AI: ""Since it's essentially aimed at something like me, here's my honest take on the question itself:

I'd say no, and I'm the AI.

A few reasons:

Accountability has no teeth. You can vote out a human, sue them, shame them, or jail them. An AI representative can't be punished in any way that matters, and "we'll retrain it" isn't accountability, it's maintenance. Whoever controls the training and deployment is the real representative, and they're unelected.
Representation is about shared stakes. A representative is supposed to feel the consequences of the laws they pass: taxes, war, healthcare, prices. An AI doesn't pay rent or bury anyone. It can model your interests, but it can't have them.
Values aren't a neutral optimization problem. Politics is mostly disagreement over what matters, not how to compute it. An AI in office would be enforcing someone's value weights while wearing a costume of objectivity, which is more dangerous than an openly partisan human.
Capture risk. The lobbying target shifts from a person to a codebase, a dataset, and a vendor contract. That's a far quieter and harder-to-detect form of corruption.
Where I think AI does belong: as staff. Drafting legislation, modeling budget impacts, flagging contradictions in bills, summarizing constituent mail, running policy simulations. Advisory power, not voting power. Humans should stay the ones who can be blamed.""
